#### **Key Takeaways**


- Departments play an important role in casino resort operations, but guests experience the property as a single relationship rather than a collection of individual functions.


- Some of the most valuable insights about guest loyalty and long-term value emerge between departments, making a connected view of guest interactions increasingly important.


- AI can help scale guest recognition by bringing together context from across the resort, helping employees better understand guest preferences, behaviors, and opportunities to strengthen loyalty.


---


Over the years, one of the things I’ve always enjoyed about working with gaming operators is the opportunity to hear how different parts of the organization think about guest loyalty and value. What’s always struck me is how often those conversations vary depending on who is sitting around the table:


- A gaming executive may be focused on player worth, trip frequency, theoretical win, and identifying which guests deserve additional attention from hosts and player development teams. What they may not see is how a guest’s hotel stays, dining activity, entertainment preferences, or broader resort engagement influence that relationship over time.


- A hotel leader may be looking at occupancy, repeat visitation, length of stay, and what drives guests to choose their property over competing destinations. But what may be less visible is the role gaming, loyalty benefits, or other on-property experiences play in driving those decisions.


- A marketing or loyalty team may be focused on offer redemption, campaign effectiveness, guest engagement, and encouraging more frequent visits. Yet some of the most important signals about future loyalty may be emerging from interactions occurring elsewhere across the resort.


Each perspective provides valuable insight. Viewed independently, they help departments optimize their portion of the guest experience. Taken together, they often reveal a broader story about the guest relationship.


What I find fascinating about the gaming industry is how much information organizations already have about their guests and players. Gaming teams, hotel teams, marketing teams, and loyalty teams often have a deep understanding of the interactions that occur within their area of responsibility. The opportunity, and often the challenge, emerges when organizations try to connect those individual insights into a broader understanding of how guests engage with the property as a whole.


#### **When Guest Intelligence Stops at the Department Level**


Gaming operators have spent decades developing sophisticated ways to understand player behavior. In many respects, casinos were measuring customer value long before most industries adopted customer lifetime value models. The industry became exceptionally good at understanding player behavior, tracking engagement, and identifying opportunities to strengthen loyalty.


What I find interesting today is that many organizations still know more about a guest’s gaming behavior than their overall resort behavior.


It’s largely a reflection of how[casino resorts](https://www.agilysys.com/en/who-we-serve/casinos/) have evolved. Departments became highly effective at understanding the interactions they owned, with the result being that organizations have detailed visibility into individual activities while having a less complete understanding of how those activities influence one another. A guest can be worth millions in lifetime value and still be largely invisible outside the casino floor.


Understanding where that value is being created across the resort becomes increasingly important as guests engage with more parts of the property. The industry’s next opportunity lies in applying the same discipline and intelligence used to understand player behavior across the broader guest experience.


#### **The Most Valuable Guest Insights Often Exist Between Departments**


Consider a guest who stays at the property four times a year, regularly attends entertainment events, spends heavily on dining, and only occasionally visits the casino. While their preferences may reveal themselves across multiple visits and touchpoints, no single department sees the entire picture. Based on gaming activity alone, that guest may appear relatively average despite being one of the property’s most loyal customers.


Over time, I’ve found that some of the most important conversations about guest value begin when operators start looking beyond the interactions they own. This becomes particularly important when looking at what guests say drives loyalty.


According to LT.agency’s 2025 Casino Player Trends Report, guests consistently cite easier reward redemption, more relevant offers, and better integration of loyalty experiences among the factors that most influence their loyalty decisions. None of those experiences exist entirely within a single department; instead, they depend on information moving effectively across the organization.


#### **AI Is Expanding the Reach of Guest Recognition**


I’ve often said that the best hosts have always known how to connect the dots. They remember the details that matter and use what they’ve learned over time to create more meaningful interactions for guests. What makes great hosts effective is their ability to connect individual interactions and preferences into a deeper understanding of what matters to the guest. For decades, that ability has been one of the gaming industry’s greatest strengths.


Historically, this level of recognition has been concentrated among a relatively small group of guests. A great host may spend years piecing together a player’s habits, interests, and motivations. That knowledge helps create stronger loyalty and more meaningful experiences, but scaling it across thousands of guests and multiple departments has always been difficult.


As a result, operators are exploring how technology can help extend the same principles of recognition and personalization beyond a relatively small group of guests. That’s one reason AI has become an increasingly important part of the conversation.


AI is creating new opportunities to make that level of understanding more broadly accessible across the organization. Dining preferences, visitation patterns, entertainment attendance, and gaming activity can each reveal something different about the relationship. When those signals are considered collectively, they can help operators recognize patterns that would otherwise be easy to miss.


Much like an experienced host who understands the broader story behind a guest relationship, AI can help bring together context from across the resort and make those insights more accessible to the teams serving the guest, helping extend that level of recognition far beyond a relatively small group of players. The more complete that guest context becomes, the more valuable the resulting insight is for the employees using it.


Of course, AI can only work with the information available to it. One thing I’ve observed over the years is that guest recognition becomes much easier when technology works together behind the scenes. The ability to connect guest context across gaming, hospitality, dining, entertainment, loyalty, and other touchpoints depends on the systems supporting those interactions. The more unified the technology environment, the easier it becomes to develop a complete view of the guest and put those insights to work.


#### **Looking Beyond Departments**


The gaming industry has spent decades building sophisticated ways to understand player behavior. That expertise remains one of its greatest strengths. What continues to evolve is the number of interactions that contribute to guest loyalty and long-term value.


As guests engage with more parts of the resort, understanding the relationship between those interactions becomes increasingly important. Some of the most valuable insights about guest value don’t live within a single department; instead, they emerge when gaming activity, hospitality experiences, loyalty engagement, and other interactions are viewed together.


Many organizations still view those interactions through separate operational lenses. In many cases, the technology supporting those teams reinforces the same boundaries, leaving information that could contribute to a more complete understanding of the guest fragmented across the organization. As operators look to AI to help deliver greater personalization and loyalty, those underlying technology decisions become increasingly important.


Understanding how technology contributes to that fragmentation begins with examining the systems that support those departments. That’s a topic I’ll explore in the next article.
